stem: The hepatic portal vein collects blood from which set of organs and delivers it to the liver?
explanation: The hepatic portal vein carries nutrient-rich blood from the stomach, small and large intestines, spleen, and pancreas to the liver for processing. This single-pass system allows the liver to metabolize absorbed nutrients and detoxify substances before they reach systemic circulation.
klp: Portal vein drains GI tract (stomach, intestines, spleen, pancreas) to liver; liver processes nutrients before systemic circulation.

stem: A patient with cirrhosis-induced portal hypertension vomits massive amounts of blood. Which portosystemic anastomosis becomes engorged to produce esophageal varices?
options: Left gastric vein anastomosing with esophageal veins
Superior mesenteric vein anastomosing with inferior vena cava
Splenic vein anastomosing with left renal vein
Inferior mesenteric vein anastomosing with systemic hemorrhoidal veins
explanation: Portal hypertension → retrograde blood flow through the left gastric (coronary) vein into esophageal submucosal veins (systemic). This portosystemic collateral becomes engorged, forming esophageal varices. Other sites: caput medusae (paraumbilical), hemorrhoids (anorectal).
klp: Esophageal varices: left gastric vein (portal) ↔ esophageal veins (systemic); most dangerous portosystemic collateral.

stem: Parietal cells, which secrete hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor, are primarily located in which region of the stomach?
explanation: Parietal cells are concentrated in the fundus and body of the stomach. They secrete HCl (via H+/K+-ATPase) and intrinsic factor. Chief cells (in fundus/body) secrete pepsinogen. G cells in the antrum secrete gastrin. Mucous neck cells produce mucus.
klp: Gastric cell types: parietal (HCl + IF, fundus/body), chief (pepsinogen, fundus/body), G cells (gastrin, antrum).

stem: Which three structures pass through the hepatoduodenal ligament (the free edge of the lesser omentum)?
options: Hepatic artery, portal vein, and bile duct
Inferior vena cava, hepatic vein, and cystic duct
Splenic artery, splenic vein, and pancreatic duct
Left gastric artery, portal vein, and thoracic duct
explanation: The hepatoduodenal ligament contains the portal triad: (1) hepatic artery proper (left), (2) common bile duct (right), and (3) portal vein (posterior). This is the site of the Pringle maneuver (manual compression to control hemorrhage).
klp: Hepatoduodenal ligament contains: portal vein, hepatic artery, and bile duct (portal triad — mnemonic: VAN = Vein, Artery, Nerve/duct).

stem: The intrinsic factor–vitamin B12 complex is absorbed in which segment of the gastrointestinal tract?
explanation: Intrinsic factor (from gastric parietal cells) binds B12 in the stomach; the complex is absorbed in the terminal ileum via cubilin receptors. Loss of parietal cells (atrophic gastritis → pernicious anemia) or terminal ileum disease (Crohn's) causes B12 deficiency and megaloblastic anemia.
klp: Vitamin B12 + intrinsic factor complex → absorbed in terminal ileum; pernicious anemia = loss of parietal cells/IF.

stem: A neonate fails to pass meconium in 48 hours. Rectal biopsy shows absence of ganglion cells in the myenteric plexus. Which embryological process failed?
options: Endodermal differentiation of the intestinal epithelium
Mesodermal formation of the muscularis externa
Neural crest cell migration into the distal intestinal wall
Fusion of the lateral plate mesoderm
explanation: Hirschsprung disease results from failure of neural crest cells to migrate into the distal colon during embryological development. The aganglionic segment cannot relax, causing functional obstruction. It is associated with RET proto-oncogene mutations and is more common in Down syndrome.
klp: Hirschsprung = failed neural crest cell migration → absent myenteric ganglion cells → aganglionic segment → obstruction.

stem: Which hormone is the primary stimulator of HCl secretion from gastric parietal cells?
explanation: Gastrin (from G cells in the gastric antrum) is the primary stimulator of HCl secretion. Histamine and acetylcholine also stimulate parietal cells. CCK stimulates pancreatic enzymes and gallbladder contraction. Secretin stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate. Somatostatin inhibits gastrin and acid secretion.
klp: Gastrin (G cells, antrum) = primary stimulator of HCl secretion; CCK = pancreatic enzymes + gallbladder; secretin = pancreatic HCO3-.

stem: After a fatty meal, which hormone stimulates both gallbladder contraction and pancreatic enzyme secretion?
explanation: CCK is released from duodenal I cells in response to fat and protein. It stimulates gallbladder contraction (bile release into duodenum) and pancreatic acinar cell enzyme secretion (lipase, amylase, proteases). It also slows gastric emptying to allow time for digestion.
klp: CCK (I cells, duodenum): released by fat/protein → gallbladder contraction + pancreatic enzyme secretion.

stem: H. pylori survives in the highly acidic stomach environment because it secretes which enzyme?
options: Urease, which converts urea to ammonia (NH3) and CO2, neutralizing local pH
Carbonic anhydrase, which produces bicarbonate to buffer acid
Catalase, which breaks down hydrogen peroxide produced by neutrophils
An exotoxin that stimulates excess HCl production
explanation: H. pylori produces urease, converting urea → NH3 + CO2. The NH3 neutralizes local gastric acid, creating a protective microenvironment. Ammonia also directly damages the mucosal epithelium. Additionally, H. pylori reduces prostaglandin synthesis (weakening the mucosal barrier) and induces inflammation.
klp: H. pylori urease → NH3 → neutralizes local acid + damages mucosa; also reduces protective prostaglandins.
audit_note: Tagged Physiology; urease is a virulence factor, so Microbiology & Immunology. Overlaps Q51 (both H. pylori).
action: Retag SEA; merge with Q51 into one case

stem: Which segment of the gastrointestinal tract is responsible for the absorption of iron and calcium?
explanation: Iron and calcium are primarily absorbed in the duodenum and proximal jejunum. Iron absorption is enhanced by vitamin C (reduces Fe3+ to Fe2+) and inhibited by phytates/tannins. Calcium absorption requires calcitriol (active vitamin D). B12 is absorbed in the terminal ileum; folate in the jejunum.
klp: Duodenum absorbs: iron (Fe2+, enhanced by vitamin C) and calcium (requires calcitriol). Terminal ileum: B12. Jejunum: folate, most nutrients.

stem: A patient with celiac disease has villous atrophy in the proximal small intestine. Which nutrient deficiency is most expected early in the disease course?
explanation: Celiac disease (immune reaction to gliadin) causes villous atrophy primarily in the duodenum and proximal jejunum. This impairs fat and fat-soluble vitamin (A, D, E, K) absorption, and also iron/calcium. Vitamin B12 is absorbed in the terminal ileum, which is typically spared early in celiac.
klp: Celiac = proximal SI villous atrophy → malabsorption of fat and fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K), iron, calcium.

stem: A patient returning from Southeast Asia has profuse watery ('rice-water') diarrhea. Vibrio cholerae is identified. What is the molecular mechanism of cholera toxin?
options: Inhibits Gi protein → decreases cAMP → decreases Cl- secretion
ADP-ribosylates Gs alpha → constitutively activates adenylate cyclase → excess cAMP → massive Cl- and water secretion
ADP-ribosylates elongation factor EF-2 → inhibits protein synthesis
Stimulates IP3/Ca2+ signaling → uncontrolled water secretion
explanation: Cholera toxin ADP-ribosylates the Gs alpha subunit, preventing GTP hydrolysis and constitutively activating adenylate cyclase → massively ↑cAMP → protein kinase A activation → phosphorylation of CFTR → Cl- efflux → osmotic water secretion. This produces watery, non-inflammatory diarrhea.
klp: Cholera toxin: ADP-ribosylates Gs → ↑cAMP → ↑Cl- secretion → massive secretory (non-bloody) diarrhea.

stem: A patient with Zollinger-Ellison syndrome has recurrent duodenal ulcers and diarrhea with steatorrhea. Which mechanism best explains the steatorrhea?
options: Gastrin directly stimulates intestinal water secretion
Excess HCl inactivates pancreatic lipase in the duodenum → fat maldigestion
Gastrin causes gallbladder hyperstimulation → bile salt diarrhea
Gastrinoma blocks CCK receptors on pancreatic acinar cells
explanation: In Zollinger-Ellison, gastrinoma → hypergastrinemia → massive HCl secretion → low duodenal pH → inactivation of pancreatic enzymes (especially lipase) → fat maldigestion → steatorrhea. The low pH also precipitates bile acids, reducing micelle formation. Multiple ulcers occur in unusual locations (e.g., jejunum).
klp: ZES: excess HCl → inactivates pancreatic lipase + precipitates bile acids → fat maldigestion + steatorrhea.

stem: In hepatic bilirubin metabolism, unconjugated bilirubin is conjugated with which compound to become water-soluble?
explanation: In the liver, bilirubin is conjugated with glucuronic acid (two molecules) by UDP-glucuronosyltransferase, forming direct (conjugated) bilirubin, which is water-soluble and excreted in bile. Albumin carries unconjugated bilirubin in the blood (unconjugated = indirect, lipid-soluble, crosses blood-brain barrier).
klp: Bilirubin conjugation: unconjugated + glucuronic acid (via UDP-glucuronosyltransferase) → conjugated (direct, water-soluble).

stem: A 22-year-old student has mild jaundice during fasting and exam stress. Lab work shows mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia with normal liver function tests and CBC. What is the most likely diagnosis and underlying defect?
options: Crigler-Najjar type I — complete absence of UDP-glucuronosyltransferase
Gilbert syndrome — reduced (not absent) UDP-glucuronosyltransferase activity
Dubin-Johnson syndrome — defective canalicular conjugated bilirubin transport
Hemolytic anemia — excess bilirubin production overwhelms normal conjugation
explanation: Gilbert syndrome (most common hereditary hyperbilirubinemia) is caused by a UGT1A1 promoter mutation reducing UDP-glucuronosyltransferase activity by ~30%. Mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia worsens with fasting, stress, or illness. It is benign with normal liver function. Crigler-Najjar type I = lethal, complete enzyme absence.
klp: Gilbert syndrome = reduced UGT1A1 activity → mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, worsens with fasting; benign, normal LFTs.

stem: A patient with alcoholic cirrhosis has an elevated PT/INR and easy bruising. Which specific biochemical defect is responsible?
options: Impaired hepatic synthesis of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X)
explanation: The liver synthesizes nearly all coagulation factors, including the vitamin K-dependent factors II (prothrombin), VII, IX, and X, and anticoagulants protein C and S. Liver disease impairs their synthesis → prolonged PT (factor VII has the shortest half-life, so PT is the most sensitive marker).
klp: Liver failure → ↓clotting factors (especially II, VII, IX, X) → prolonged PT; factor VII has shortest half-life, PT rises first.

stem: A patient with hereditary hemochromatosis has elevated serum ferritin and transferrin saturation. The liver is the central organ controlling systemic iron levels via which hormone?
explanation: Hepcidin (produced by the liver) is the master regulator of iron homeostasis. High iron → ↑hepcidin → binds and degrades ferroportin on enterocytes and macrophages → ↓iron absorption and release. In hereditary hemochromatosis (HFE gene mutation), hepcidin is inappropriately low → unregulated iron absorption.
klp: Hepcidin (liver) is the master iron regulator; degrades ferroportin → ↓iron absorption; hemochromatosis = low hepcidin → iron overload.
audit_note: Hemochromatosis is not named in the blueprint; fits under GI-8 (minerals).

stem: Phenylketonuria (PKU) is caused by deficiency of which enzyme, and what is the inheritance pattern?
explanation: PKU results from autosomal recessive deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH), which converts phenylalanine → tyrosine. Accumulated phenylalanine → phenylketones (phenylpyruvate, phenylacetate) → musty body odor and intellectual disability if untreated. Screened at birth; treated with phenylalanine-restricted diet.
klp: PKU = phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency (AR) → accumulate phenylalanine → phenylketones → intellectual disability; musty odor.
audit_note: The blueprint lists PKU under Neurological, not Gastrointestinal.
action: Retag system; rewrite as a case

stem: Which hepatitis virus is transmitted via the fecal-oral route and does NOT cause chronic infection?
explanation: HAV (ssRNA, picornavirus) is transmitted via contaminated food/water (fecal-oral). It causes self-limiting acute hepatitis with no chronic phase and no carrier state. HBV, HCV, and HDV can all cause chronic infection. HEV is also fecal-oral but can cause chronic infection in immunocompromised patients.
klp: HAV: fecal-oral, acute self-limiting, no chronic infection. HBV/HCV: parenteral/sexual, can be chronic. HEV: fecal-oral, can be chronic in immunocompromised.
audit_note: Negative stem (does NOT). Board items avoid these. Overlaps Q50.

stem: Which hepatitis virus requires co-infection with hepatitis B virus in order to infect and replicate?
explanation: Hepatitis D (delta virus) is an RNA satellite virus that requires HBsAg from hepatitis B virus to form its envelope. HDV can occur as co-infection (simultaneous HBV+HDV, usually self-limiting) or superinfection (HDV in a chronic HBV carrier → severe, often fulminant hepatitis).
klp: HDV requires HBV co-infection; superinfection (HDV into chronic HBV carrier) = worst prognosis, fulminant hepatitis.

stem: H. pylori is best classified as which type of organism?
explanation: H. pylori is a gram-negative, microaerophilic (requires reduced O2), flagellated spiral/helical rod. Key virulence factors: urease, CagA toxin, VacA cytotoxin, flagella. It colonizes the gastric mucus layer and antrum. Diagnosed by urea breath test, stool antigen, or biopsy urease test.
klp: H. pylori: gram-negative, microaerophilic, spiral rod; urease-positive; causes PUD, gastric adenocarcinoma, MALT lymphoma.

stem: A 7-year-old develops bloody diarrhea after eating undercooked hamburger, followed by oliguria and pallor. Lab shows microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and elevated creatinine. Which toxin caused this syndrome and how does it work?
options: Cholera toxin — ADP-ribosylates Gs to increase cAMP
Shiga-like toxin (EHEC) — cleaves 28S rRNA of 60S ribosome, inhibiting protein synthesis
Exfoliatin toxin (S. aureus) — cleaves desmoglein 1 in the skin
TSST-1 — superantigen activating T cells nonspecifically
explanation: EHEC (E. coli O157:H7) produces Shiga-like toxin (verotoxin) which cleaves 28S rRNA of the 60S ribosomal subunit, halting protein synthesis. Endothelial damage causes the triad of hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS): microangiopathic hemolytic anemia + thrombocytopenia + acute renal failure. Antibiotics are contraindicated (increase toxin release).
klp: EHEC (O157:H7) Shiga-like toxin → inhibits 60S ribosome → endothelial damage → HUS (hemolytic anemia + thrombocytopenia + renal failure).
audit_note: Shiga toxin removes an adenine from 28S rRNA (N-glycosidase); cleaves is loose wording.

stem: A biopsy from a Crohn's patient shows non-caseating granulomas. Which immune cells are the primary cellular components of these granulomas?
options: Epithelioid macrophages surrounded by Th1 CD4+ T cells
explanation: Granulomas form through Type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity: Th1 CD4+ cells secrete IFN-γ → activates macrophages → epithelioid cells + Langhans giant cells (fused macrophages). These aggregate into granulomas. Crohn's granulomas are non-caseating (vs. TB which is caseating).
klp: Granulomas = epithelioid macrophages + Th1 CD4+ T cells (Type IV hypersensitivity); Crohn's = non-caseating; TB = caseating.

stem: Which feature correctly distinguishes Salmonella from Shigella gastroenteritis?
options: Shigella has an animal reservoir; Salmonella does not
Salmonella is associated with poultry/eggs and can cause bacteremia; Shigella is limited to the gut and is person-to-person
Shigella causes watery diarrhea; Salmonella causes bloody dysentery
Salmonella is gram-positive; Shigella is gram-negative
explanation: Salmonella: animal reservoir (poultry, eggs, reptiles), can invade bloodstream (bacteremia, typhoid fever), produces H2S. Shigella: human-only reservoir, transmitted person-to-person (very low infectious dose), limited to colon, produces Shiga toxin. Both are gram-negative rods. Shigella causes bloody dysentery; Salmonella may cause watery or bloody diarrhea.
klp: Salmonella: poultry/eggs, bacteremia possible, animal reservoir. Shigella: person-to-person, no bacteremia, human-only reservoir, very low ID50.

stem: Which feature correctly distinguishes Crohn's disease from ulcerative colitis?
options: Crohn's is limited to the colon; UC can affect any part of the GI tract
Crohn's shows transmural inflammation with skip lesions; UC shows mucosal/submucosal inflammation from rectum continuously
UC is associated with non-caseating granulomas; Crohn's is not
Crohn's has a higher risk of colorectal cancer than UC
explanation: Crohn's: transmural inflammation (all layers), skip lesions, any segment from mouth to anus, non-caseating granulomas, cobblestone appearance, fistulas/strictures. UC: mucosal/submucosal only, continuous from rectum proximally, pseudopolyps, higher colorectal cancer risk, no granulomas.
klp: Crohn's: transmural + skip lesions + granulomas + any GI segment. UC: mucosal + continuous from rectum + higher CRC risk + pseudopolyps.

stem: An alcoholic with cirrhosis develops a distended abdomen. Paracentesis reveals straw-colored fluid with a serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) >1.1. What is the primary mechanism of ascites formation in this patient?
options: Portal hypertension and hypoalbuminemia causing fluid shift into peritoneal cavity
Increased renal aldosterone secretion causing direct peritoneal exudation
explanation: Cirrhotic ascites has two primary mechanisms: (1) Portal hypertension → increased hydrostatic pressure in splanchnic circulation → fluid extravasation; (2) Decreased hepatic albumin synthesis → reduced oncotic pressure → fluid accumulates in peritoneum. SAAG >1.1 indicates portal hypertension as the cause (vs. <1.1 = non-portal cause, e.g., malignancy).
klp: Cirrhotic ascites: portal hypertension + hypoalbuminemia → fluid shift into peritoneum; SAAG >1.1 confirms portal HTN.

stem: A patient with a 15-year history of GERD undergoes endoscopy showing salmon-colored mucosa replacing squamous epithelium in the distal esophagus. Biopsy confirms intestinal metaplasia (goblet cells). Which complication does this predispose to?
options: Squamous cell carcinoma of the esophagus
explanation: Barrett's esophagus = replacement of normal squamous epithelium with intestinal-type columnar epithelium (goblet cells) due to chronic acid reflux → metaplasia → dysplasia → adenocarcinoma. Squamous cell carcinoma of the esophagus is associated with tobacco and alcohol, arising in the upper/middle third.
klp: Barrett's esophagus: columnar metaplasia from GERD → risk of esophageal adenocarcinoma (distal/GEJ); SCC linked to tobacco+alcohol.

stem: A 68-year-old male presents with painless jaundice, significant weight loss, and a palpable non-tender gallbladder (Courvoisier's sign). Which diagnosis is most consistent with these findings?
explanation: Courvoisier's sign (painless jaundice + palpable non-tender gallbladder) indicates malignant obstruction of the CBD, most commonly from pancreatic head adenocarcinoma. In choledocholithiasis, the gallbladder is typically scarred and fibrotic (non-palpable). Pancreatic cancer is often associated with CA 19-9 elevation and has a poor prognosis (only ~20% resectable).
klp: Courvoisier's sign: painless jaundice + palpable gallbladder = malignant CBD obstruction (pancreatic head cancer, not stones).

stem: Sporadic colorectal cancer most commonly develops via which genetic sequence?
options: MLH1/MSH2 mismatch repair mutations → microsatellite instability
APC → K-ras → SMAD4 → TP53 mutations (adenoma-carcinoma sequence)
CDKN2A loss → RB phosphorylation → uncontrolled proliferation
explanation: Sporadic CRC follows the adenoma-carcinoma sequence with chromosomal instability: APC mutation (initiates adenoma) → K-ras mutation (promotes growth) → SMAD4/18q loss (progression) → TP53 loss (malignant conversion). MLH1/MSH2 mutations cause Lynch syndrome (microsatellite instability pathway, ~15% of CRC).
klp: Sporadic CRC: APC → K-ras → SMAD4 → TP53 (adenoma-carcinoma sequence). Lynch syndrome: MMR gene mutations → microsatellite instability.

stem: A 45-year-old female with progressive pruritus and jaundice has elevated alkaline phosphatase and positive anti-mitochondrial antibodies (AMA). Which cells are the primary target of this autoimmune disease?
explanation: Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) is an autoimmune disease targeting intrahepatic cholangiocytes (bile duct epithelial cells), causing progressive cholestasis and eventually cirrhosis. AMA (especially anti-M2, targeting pyruvate dehydrogenase complex) is the hallmark in >90% of cases. It primarily affects middle-aged women.
klp: PBC: autoimmune destruction of intrahepatic cholangiocytes → cholestasis; AMA positive (anti-M2); middle-aged women.
audit_note: Primary biliary cholangitis is not named in the blueprint; fits under cholestasis.
